notes.text: Was a child — In the infancy of Israel. I loved him - Manifested my tender and paternal affection to him. Called my son - Adopted him to be my son, and as my son, provided for him, and brought him out of servitude. Out of Egypt - But Israel, the first adopted son was a type of Christ the first-born. And the history of Israel's coming out was a type of Christ's future coming out of Egypt.

They — Moses and Aaron, and other prophets. Called - Persuaded, intreated, and urged by exhortations, the whole house of Israel. From them - From the prophets counsel and commands. Baalim - In the desert they began this apostacy, and held on with obstinacy in it.
I taught — As a mother or nurse helps the child. Taking them - Supporting and bearing them up. They knew not - They would not see nor acknowledge me in it.

Cords of man — With such kindness as best fits and most prevails with a man. I was to them - As a careful husband-man in due season takes the yoke from his labouring oxen, and takes off the muzzle with which they were kept from eating, when at work. I laid meat unto them - Brought them provision in their wants.
He — Ephraim. Shall be king - Shall rule them with rigor and cruelty. They refused - The reason of all is, their obstinacy in idolatry.
His branches — The lesser towns and villages. Their own counsels - Which they have followed in opposition to all the good counsels the prophets gave them from time to time.
They — The prophets. None at all - Scarce any one would hearken and obey.

Give thee up — To utter destruction. Admah and Zeboim were two of the four cities which were destroyed with fire from heaven. My repentings - Not that God is ever fluctuating or unresolved; but these are expressions after the manner of men, to shew what severity Israel had deserved, and yet how divine grace would be glorified in sparing them.

Return — Conquerors that plunder the conquered city, carry away the wealth of it, and after some time return to burn it; God will not do so. Not man - Therefore my compassions fail not. The holy One - A holy God, and in covenant, though not with all, yet with many among you. Enter into the city - Utterly to destroy thee, as I did Sodom.

They — The remnant shall hear and obey the Lord. Like a lion - The word of the Lord, so saith the Chaldee, shall roar as a lion. Christ is called, The lion of the tribe of Judah: and when he cried with a loud voice, it was as when a lion roared. The voice of the gospel was heard far, as the roaring of a lion; and it was a mighty voice. Tremble - The spirit by its power awakening them to a sight of sin, shall make them fear and tremble. From the west - From the ends of the earth.

They shall tremble — At their return into their own land, some shall hasten, yet with solicitude, out of Egypt, whither they fled for shelter; others like doves shall hasten out of Assyria, but with fear and trembling. I will place them - A seasonable and comfortable promise.
Gathered — Into their own land.
No city — Or rather, no town inhabited, where they might refresh themselves.
The Lord — Hebrew. Unto Jehovah, to the true God. For the Heathens had, many of them, some knowledge of the true God.
Forth — Out of the wilderness.

glossa.text:
*Give praise to the Lord.* ((ID.)) This psalm teaches what we are through ourselves, etc., *as far as* he first admonishes the redeemed to give praise. *Give praise.*

((CASS., AUG.)) Of which there are seven divisions, etc., *as far as* in the seventh he treats of heretics, there, *And they were made few.*
*And from the sea.* ((CASS.)) For the south he puts the sea, understanding thereby the ocean of that quarter; and this can be taken for any quarter of the world whatever.
*They wandered.* ((ID.)) The second part, where is the first temptation, etc., *as far as* fourthly, confession for having been heard, that is, praise.

*Hungry.* ((AUG.)) He signifies the curious of the world, who sought out the truth by divers opinions, and found it not. *Their soul,* etc. God commends himself, because it is expedient for us; we fail that we may ask, and may love him who comes to our aid.

*And he led.* ((AUG.)) As it were, he rescued them from ignorance, showing the way, Christ. Behold, he freed them from error; but in what manner he freed them from the hunger and thirst wherewith they burned, he will say afterwards; but he sets confession first.
*Wonderful things.* ((HIER.)) As it were, in a wonderful manner of redemption were the mercies given.

*Him that is hungry.* ((CASS.)) Him that desires to know, or him that desires not to know, but fails through too great fasting, as is wont to befall one worn out by too great hunger or by infirmity, so that he desires not to eat, but fails through too great fasting.

*Sitting.* ((AUG.)) The third part, where the second temptation is set down, etc., *as far as* let us also consider that we can do this.

*Who is wise, and will keep these things?* ((ID.)) The conclusion, as if he should say: since the Lord helps the poor man, therefore: *Who is wise? The mercies.* That he delivers from error, etc., *as far as* and the unjust shall stop his mouth.

notes.text: If ye are risen, seek the things above — As Christ being risen, immediately went to heaven.

For ye are dead — To the things on earth. And your real, spiritual life is hid from the world, and laid up in God, with Christ - Who hath merited, promised, prepared it for us, and gives us the earnest and foretaste of it in our hearts.
When Christ — The abruptness of the sentence surrounds us with sudden light. Our life - The fountain of holiness and glory. Shall appear - In the clouds of heaven.

Mortify therefore — Put to death, slay with a continued stroke. Your members - Which together make up the body of sin. Which are upon the earth - Where they find their nourishment. Uncleanness - In act, word, or thought. Inordinate affection - Every passion which does not flow from and lead to the love of God. Evil desire - The desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life. Covetousness - According to the derivation of the word, means the desire of having more, or of any thing independent on God. Which is idolatry - Properly and directly; for it is giving the heart to a creature.
For which — Though the heathens lightly regarded them.
Living denotes the inward principle; walking, the outward acts.

Wrath — Is lasting anger. Filthy discourse - And was there need to warn even these saints of God against so gross and palpable a sin as this? O what is man, till perfect love casts out both fear and sin.
In knowledge — The knowledge of God, his will, his word.

Where — In which case, it matters not what a man is externally, whether Jew or gentile, circumcised, or uncircumcised, barbarian, void of all the advantages of education, yea, Scythian, of all barbarians most barbarous. But Christ is in all that are thus renewed, and is all things in them and to them.

glossa.text: *The things that are above.* Not by place, but by merit of excellence.
*The things above.* Spiritual things, which were signified through the carnal observances, these are eternal glory and the things which lead to it.

*Your life hidden.* That is, your time has not yet come, because the summer has not yet come, that is, the coming of Christ, where the fruitful trees shall be discerned from the barren; but the time of those who love earthly things is always ready. But when Christ shall have appeared, this is our time.

*Mortify,* etc. After the reasonings concerning the fulness of Christ, a general exhortation to all concerning morals is subjoined, lest they return to their former habit. *Your members.* That is, the parts of the old man, or the concupiscences of the members. *Fornication,* etc. He describes the offences which he calls members, that after receiving the reason of truth they might give their labour to a good life. It much harms to know the reason of the true, and not to carry it out in deeds. *For he who knows the will of the Lord, and does not do it, shall be beaten with many stripes ((Luc. XII))*. *And covetousness.* Under one name he forbids two most evil things, idolatry and covetousness, which is not a dissimilar wickedness, because it is the root of all evils, and they are fulfilled in almost one work: because, as idolatry strives to take glory away from the one God, lest he alone should have the name of deity, so the covetous man extends himself into the things of God, that he alone may usurp what God made for all: both are hostile to God, because they deny to God the things which are his.
*In which you also walked.* He mentions this, that they may rejoice that they have escaped, and may beware for the rest.

*But now.* Above he forbade the graver things, now the lesser, lest these be thought not dangerous. There are those who have not the habit of drunkenness, who sometimes get drunk: as also there are those who have not the habit of lying, and yet sometimes lie, so it happens in other matters also. He forbids therefore to lie sometimes, and especially to lie continually.

*Who is renewed.* The renewal of the mind is said to be according to God, as is read in the epistle to the Ephesians, or *according to the image of God,* as is read here. But it is said according to God for this reason, lest it be thought to come about according to some other creature.

notes.text: Who made me a judge? — In worldly things. His kingdom is not of this world.
He said to them — Perhaps to the two brothers, and through them to the people. A man's life - That is, the comfort or happiness of it.
What shall I do? — The very language of want! Do? Why, lay up treasure in heaven.
Thou fool — To think of satisfying thy soul with earthly goods! To depend on living many years! Yea, one day! They - The messengers of death, commissioned by God, require thy soul of thee!
Rich toward God — Namely, in faith, and love, and good works.

glossa.text: *Master.* Upon one who was commending the grace of the peace and unity above, this man wishes to thrust the trouble of an earthly division; whence also he is called a man, that is, earthly. For those among whom there is a zeal and contention of this kind are men, and walk according to man. Among brethren it is not a judge in the midst but family affection as arbitress that ought to divide a patrimony, although the patrimony of immortality is not money to be sought by men.

*Who hath appointed me.* I am not the God of dissension but of peace and unity, who came to make men at peace with the angels, that many may have one heart and one soul. Not that they may be divided, but that they may have all things in common, and that there be not anyone in need among them. He who does not gather with me is a divider of brotherhood and an author of dissension.

*Of all covetousness.* No one would think it a crime to divide an inheritance, to gather fruits into barns; but the judge above declares that this too is covetousness, whence also he adds: *of a certain rich man.* As above against the Pharisees and hypocrites, so here, on the occasion of a foolish petition, he disputes against covetousness. *Not in abundance. Man liveth not by bread alone, but in the word of God ((Deut. VIII))* , nor is temporal life prolonged by a multitude of riches.

*And he spoke,* etc. After the precept he subjoins an example for the avoiding of covetousness for temporal things. *The plentiful fruits of a certain rich man.* The rich man is not blamed because he tilled the ground, or laid up his fruits in barns, but because he placed the confidence of his life in them, and did not lay them out upon the poor, that he might be received by them into everlasting dwellings.

*What shall I do,* etc. Reckoning the fruits to be his own and the goods his own, he does not lay out upon the poor what is over and above, but is eager to keep it for his own luxury against the time to come, and knows not who will make use of what he has gathered.

*My goods, and I will say. ((AMBR.))* Those are not a man's goods which he cannot carry away with him. For mercy alone is the companion of the dead.

*Take thy rest.* Behold, to the plague of covetousness is joined the plague of sloth, so that he did not even call upon God for temporal things.

*But he said.* For God to speak is to check a man's depraved contrivances by a sudden chastisement. *Thou fool.* Because thou wast promising thyself long seasons of riches, this night, snatched away, thou shalt leave to others what thou hast gathered. *They require,* etc. In the night the soul is taken away, which in the darkness of the heart would not foresee what it could suffer.

*And is not rich toward God.* He is rich toward God who, despising things transitory, distributes to the poor; whose expectation is the Lord; whose substance, that is, the possession of a conscience by which he is sustained and fed, is with God, not in the purses of earth.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: "Where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God" verbally echoes the LXX of Ps 110:1 ("Sit at my right hand"), the most-cited OT verse in the NT. High volume of distinctive language (right hand, seated, exaltation) and strong recurrence make the session at God's right hand the dominant figure for the exalted Christ. Coherence with Colossians' cosmic Christology is exact.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The exalted Christ glorified and revealed in heavenly session may faintly invoke Daniel's Son of Man given dominion and glory before the Ancient of Days. Low volume since no distinctive vocabulary is reproduced; the echo rests on the shared schema of heavenly enthronement and future revelation "in glory" (v.4).

echoes.text: You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory. Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
echoes.note: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God" coheres with the psalmist's hope that God is his portion and will receive him to glory, the hidden security of life bound to God. Faint and contested; rests on thematic coherence (hiddenness, glory, God as the believer's life) rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: "Covetousness, which is idolatry" presupposes the Decalogue's prohibition of coveting, the climactic command that exposes disordered desire. The identification of greed with idolatry draws on Israel's covenant logic where craving what is not one's own is functionally false worship; coherent with Second-Temple Jewish moralizing of pleonexia.

echoes.text: “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
echoes.note: Naming covetousness "idolatry" invokes the first commandment's exclusive worship and the prohibition of other gods. The equation of greed with idol-service is a recurring Second-Temple move (cf. Testament traditions) grounded in the Decalogue's opening; coheres with the wrath-of-God indictment that follows.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: "Evil desire" and the inventory of corrupt members recall the prophetic-Pentateuchal diagnosis that the inclination of the human heart is only evil continually. Faint; the vice list is a Hellenistic-Jewish form and contact is conceptual (the earthly members, depraved passion) rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Remember, and don’t forget, how you provoked Yahweh your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day that you left the land of Egypt, until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against Yahweh.
echoes.note: "The wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience" coheres with Deuteronomy's recurring theme of divine wrath provoked by Israel's rebellion and idolatry. Faint and generic; the wrath-against-disobedience schema is pervasive across the prophets, so no single passage controls.

echoes.text: Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab; for they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods. The people ate and bowed down to their gods. Israel joined himself to Baal Peor. Yahweh’s anger was kindled against Israel. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take all the chiefs of the people, and hang them up to Yahweh before the sun, that the fierce anger of Yahweh may turn away from Israel.” Moses said to […]
echoes.note: Linking sexual immorality and idolatry, followed by divine wrath, echoes the Baal-Peor episode where harlotry with Moab and idol-worship together kindle God's anger. Faint; contact is the recurrent OT pairing of porneia with idolatry under wrath rather than verbal citation.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: "The new man, being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator" directly reworks the creation of humanity in God's image. High volume (image, Creator, the making of man) and exact coherence: the new self is re-creation according to the imago Dei, recapitulating Gen 1. Availability and recurrence in Pauline new-creation theology are strong.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not steal. “‘You shall not lie. “‘You shall not deceive one another.
echoes.note: "Don't lie to one another" closely tracks the Holiness Code's "you shall not lie one to another" (LXX), addressed to the covenant community. Strong verbal and situational coherence (reciprocal prohibition among the people of God); the holiness framing fits Colossians' renewed humanity.

echoes.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness.
echoes.note: "After the image of his Creator" also resonates with the toledot statement that God made man in his likeness, the verse that reasserts the image after the fall. Supports the renewal-of-the-image reading; medium because Gen 1:26-27 is the primary lexical source and 5:1 is the secondary, reinforcing one.

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: "There can't be Greek and Jew... but Christ is all and in all" figurally reconstitutes the single humanity created in God's image, undoing the divisions of the nations. The renewed image (vv.10) grounds a restored one-humanity; coheres with Gen 1's making of mankind as a unity before the scattering of Babel.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard the voice of Yahweh God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden. Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I […]
echoes.note: "Put off the old man... put on the new" with its clothing imagery may figurally invoke Adam: the garments and the postlapsarian self stripped off. Faint and contested; the old-man/new-man Adam typology is conceptual, and the clothing metaphor is widely diffused in Jewish moral discourse.

echoes.text: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said one to another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole […]
echoes.note: The catalog of peoples (Greek, Jew, barbarian, Scythian) reconciled in Christ faintly reverses Babel's scattering and confusion of tongues into many nations. Low volume; the reversal-of-Babel reading is thematic and contested, resting on the restoration of one humanity rather than any cited wording.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?'—the Hebrew's rebuke of Moses—is verbally echoed in Jesus' 'Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?' The near-quotation of the question gives notable Volume, though the speaker roles are inverted, marking it a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
echoes.note: 'Whoever loves money will not be satisfied with money'—Qoheleth's verdict on the futility of abundance—coheres directly with 'a man's life doesn't consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.' The wisdom critique of accumulation supports the warning against covetousness.

echoes.text: If a man has two wives, the one beloved, and the other hated, and they have borne him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son is hers who was hated; then it shall be, in the day that he causes his sons to inherit that which he has, that he may not give the son of the beloved the rights of the firstborn before the son of the hated, who is the firstborn; but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated, by giving him a […]
echoes.note: The Torah law of inheritance division among heirs supplies the legal backdrop for the brother's request to divide the inheritance. It is the unstated Availability rather than an allusion Luke develops, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: There is that waxes rich by his wariness and pinching, And this is the portion of his reward: When he says, I have found rest, And now will I eat of my goods; Yet he knows not what time will pass, And he will leave them to others, and die.
echoes.note: Ben Sira describes one who grows rich, says 'I have found rest, now I will enjoy my goods,' yet does not know his death is near and must leave them to others. This is the closest Second-Temple template for the rich fool: the inner monologue of ease, the unexpected death, and the unanswered 'whose will they be,' giving very high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's refrain that there is nothing better than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment underlies the rich fool's 'take your ease, eat, drink, be merry.' Luke ironizes the wisdom counsel by exposing its folly when death intervenes, giving strong thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
echoes.note: 'I commend enjoyment, for man has nothing better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry' is virtually quoted in the fool's resolve. The verbal triad eat/drink/be merry makes this a direct verbal source, though Luke subverts it.

echoes.text: “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.
echoes.note: 'He heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather it' is closely echoed by God's 'the things you have prepared—whose will they be?' The psalm's lament over the futility of hoarding against death gives strong Coherence and good Volume.

echoes.text: As the partridge that sits on eggs which she has not laid, so is he who gets riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days they shall leave him, and at his end he shall be a fool.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's proverb that one who gets riches unjustly will leave them in the midst of his days and prove a fool at his end supplies both the 'fool' verdict and the premature loss of wealth. The shared fool-and-forfeited-riches motif gives notable Coherence.

echoes.text: For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
echoes.note: 'What is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?' parallels the question posed to the rich man whose soul is required. The taking of the life of the prosperous-but-godless undergirds the parable's verdict.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him. Though while he lived he blessed his soul— and men praise you when you do well for yourself— he shall go to the generation of his fathers. They shall never see the light. A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.
echoes.note: The psalm warns not to fear the rich who lay up wealth, for they carry nothing away at death and perish like the beasts. The 'man in his pomp who does not understand' is a near-portrait of the rich fool, giving good Coherence to 'not rich toward God.'

echoes.text: “If I have made gold my hope, and have said to the fine gold, ‘You are my confidence;’ If I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because my hand had gotten much; if I have seen the sun when it shined, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for I should have denied the God who is above.
echoes.note: Job's disavowal of making gold his hope reflects the parable's contrast between trusting accumulated wealth and being 'rich toward God.' The trust-in-riches-as-folly theme is a coherent but lighter echo.

echoes.text: Wakefulness that comes of riches consumes the flesh, And the anxiety thereof puts away sleep. Wakeful anxiety will crave slumber; And in a sore disease sleep will be broken. A rich man toileth in gathering money together; And when he rests, he is filled with his good things. A poor man toileth in lack of substance; And when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's reflections on wealth, sleepless anxiety over riches, and the rare rich man who is blameless complement the parable's critique of storing goods. A faint Second-Temple coherence echo behind the barn-building scheme.

notes.text: The method of it. For whereas there are some passages in it which seem impious; it must be considered, that it is in part dramatical; that Solomon speaks most things in his own name, but some things in the names of ungodly men, as is undeniably manifest both front the scope and design of the book, as it is expressed both in the beginning and in the conclusion of it, and from his serious and large disputation against those wicked principles and courses. And this way of writing is not unusual among both sacred and profane writers.

I was king — Having asserted the vanity of all things in the general, he now comes to prove his assertion in those particulars wherein men commonly seek, and with greatest probability expect to find, true happiness. He begins with secular wisdom. And to shew how competent a judge he was of this matter, he lays down this character, That he was the preacher, which implies eminent knowledge; and a king, who therefore had all imaginable opportunities and advantages for the attainment of happiness, and particularly for the getting of wisdom, by consulting all sorts of books and men, by trying all manner of experiments; and no ordinary king, but king over Israel, God's own people, a wise and an happy people, whose king he was by God's special appointment and furnished by God, with singular wisdom for that great trust; and whose abode was in Jerusalem where were the house of God and the most wise and learned of the priests attending upon it, and the seats of justice, and colleges or assemblies of the wisest men of their nation. All these concurring in him, which rarely do in any other men, make the argument drawn from his experience more convincing.

I gave my heart — Which phrase denotes his serious and fixed purpose, and his great industry in it. To search - To seek diligently and accurately. By wisdom - By the help of that wisdom wherewith God had endowed me. Concerning - Concerning all the works of God and men in this lower world; the works of nature; the works of Divine providence; and the works and depths of human policy. This travel - This difficult and toilsome work of searching out these things, God hath inflicted as a just punishment upon man for his eating of the tree of knowledge. To be exercised - To employ themselves in the painful study of these things.
Seen — Diligently observed. Vanity - Not only unsatisfying, but also an affliction or breaking to a man's spirit.
All my labour — All these riches and buildings, and other fruits of my labour, were aggravations of my misery. Because - Because I must, and that everlastingly, leave them all behind me.
Or a fool — Who will undo all that I have done, and turn the effects of my wisdom into instruments of his folly. Some think he had such an opinion of Rehoboam.
Despair — I gave myself up to despair of ever reaping that satisfaction which I promised to myself.

Wisdom — Who uses great industry, and prudence, and justice too, in the use and management of his affairs. To a man - Who has spent his days in sloth and folly. A great evil - A great disorder in itself, and a great torment to a considering mind.
For what — What comfort or benefit remains to any man after this short and frail life is once ended?

Sorrows — Full of sorrows. Tho' he took great and unwearied pains all his days, yet the toils of his body were accompanied with vexation of mind. His heart - Because his sleep was broken with perplexing cares.

glossa.text:
*Vanity of vanities.* ((ID.)) For *vanity of vanities*, according to certain interpreters, we can say, etc., *as far as* until that come which is perfect.

Before he sets down his own statement, he seems to make a kind of preparation and adornment, when he says: *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.* Afterwards he begins from the greater, that is, from man, showing him subject to vanity, that is, to mutability. And this is, *vanity,* etc. Every man living is vanity: how much more the rest! Whence, *The creature is made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who,* etc. For whatever is able not to be can be called vanity, because it is able to be changed. God alone is always the same that he is. But that which is changed in some manner vanishes away, and is not what it was; in comparison with the Creator, every creature can be called vanity and be reckoned as it were nothing.

((HIER.)) If all the things which God made, etc., *as far as* I am compelled to say not once, but twice, *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.*

*And I proposed in my mind,* etc. Ecclesiastes therefore proposed, etc., *as far as* which they incurred of their own accord.

Thus far generally concerning the vanities of the age: from here he returns to himself, and shows who he was, how he came to know all things, and how he taught them, whence: *And I proposed in my mind,* and the rest.

*This occupation.* ((HIER.)) The word *anian* Aquila, the LXX and Theodotion [render] περισπασμὸν, which in Latin is *distensio,* etc., *as far as* all things are referred to the higher sense.

*I saw,* etc. I considered all worldly things, and saw that there is vanity and malice, that is, the miseries of the spirit, by which the mind, wearied with diverse thoughts, labours to know that which is not granted to man.

((HIER.)) The word *Routh* Aquila and Theodotion, etc., *as far as* by which the soul is afflicted with diverse thoughts.

*Again I detested.* ((HIER.)) By spiritual labour the saints meditate day and night in the law of the Lord, etc., *as far as* for it is not wisdom to gather earthly riches.

*Being about to have.* This befell Solomon himself, who had a son Roboam not like himself. From which we understand that a son is not even worthy of his father's inheritance, if he be foolish.
*For when another.* ((ID.)) Above, concerning the uncertain heir, etc., *as far as* from reason.

notes.text: I will — I will hearken what God by his Spirit speaks to me, and that will I now speak to you. A parable - Which properly is an allegorical speech, but is often taken for an important, and withal, dark doctrine or sentence. Open - I will not smother it in my own breast, but publish it to the world. Dark - So he calls the following discourse, because the thing in question ever hath been thought hard to be understood.

In the days — In times of great distress and calamity, when wicked men flourish, and good men are oppressed. Supplanters - This character fitly agrees to David's enemies, who were not only malicious, but deceitful and treacherous.

Trust — As that which will secure them from calamities. Having said that good men had no cause of fear, from their present sufferings from ungodly men, now he proceeds to shew, that the ungodly had no reason to be secure because of their riches.
Redeem — Neither from the first death, nor from the second. Brother - Whom he would do his utmost to preserve.
Soul — Of their life. Precious - Hard to be obtained. Ceaseth - It is never to be accomplished, by any mere man, for himself or for his brother.

He seeth — Every man sees that all men die, the wise and the foolish; the evil and the good. To others - He saith not to sons or kindred; but to others, because he is wholly uncertain to whom he shall leave them, to friends, or strangers, or enemies; which he mentions as a great vanity in riches. They neither can save them from death, nor will accompany him in and after death; and after his death will be disposed, he knows not how, nor to whom.

Thought — Tho' they are ashamed to express, yet it is their secret hope. Houses - Either their posterity, often called mens houses: or their mansion-houses, as it is explained in the next clause. For ever - To them and theirs in succeeding generations. Call - Fondly dreaming by this means to immortalize their memories.
Man — Living in all splendour and glory. Abideth not - All his dreams of perpetuating his name and estate, shall be confuted by experience.

glossa.text: *Hate these things, all ye nations.* ((CASS.)) I except none, etc., *as far as* when, namely, the cockle shall be separated from the wheat, the sheep from the goats.
*And ye that are earthborn.* (((AUG.)) I withhold my speech from none, let the heir of the earth hear, because of the judgment: the just man, because of the kingdom.
*My mouth shall speak.* ((CASS.)) He commends the things to be said. *Wisdom* for divine things, *Prudence* for instructing morals; in these two the whole divine discourse is signified.
*I will incline.* ((HIER.)) I will humble myself to the truth speaking within, which teaches to speak in parables, lest it lie open to all.

*Why shall I fear.* ((CASS.)) He begins to narrate the things he promised, saying that Christ will not redeem the ungodly; here the prophet, in his own person pleading a general cause, seeks the cause of the damnation and the fear of the wicked, which is iniquity. ((AUG.)) Why shall I fear? as though there is not what I should fear, since to avoid iniquity is in my own power; for that alone shall there be fear in the last day, which shall be evil to the damned, not to the just. *Of the heel. ((Ibid.))* He alludes to the words, etc., *as far as* that is, it shall oppress and shall make to fear.
*They that trust.* These, namely, who trust, etc., *as far as* in which they are so foolish.
*A brother doth not redeem.* If a brother, that is Christ, does not redeem, etc., *as far as* because such a one gives not to God a propitiation.

*And shall live still. ((Ibid.))* After the end of life, he shall live according to the soul, because the soul shall not perish with the body, but shall be saved unto grief, until, the body being received, he be tormented on both sides.

*He shall not see. ((Ibid.))* That is, he does not understand, etc., *as far as* when the wise man passes through life. Or, *the unwise. ((Ibid.))* Who attends not. *The fool.* Who, if he attends, does not beware. *Riches* ((CASS.)) For the sake of which they did evil. *His own:* which are not according to God.
*They have called their names.* ((AUG.)) The heirs, who at the sepulchres of the dead make themselves drunk in memory of them, but neither does a drop reach the tongue of him that burns in hell.

*And man when.* And both in this, and in the rest, man does not understand; or, therefore God is not to be accused, he understood not his own dignity, he acted not understandingly, but was compared, reason being lost, to beasts, not in another thing, but in wisdom.

notes.text: If ye are risen, seek the things above — As Christ being risen, immediately went to heaven.

For ye are dead — To the things on earth. And your real, spiritual life is hid from the world, and laid up in God, with Christ - Who hath merited, promised, prepared it for us, and gives us the earnest and foretaste of it in our hearts.
When Christ — The abruptness of the sentence surrounds us with sudden light. Our life - The fountain of holiness and glory. Shall appear - In the clouds of heaven.

Mortify therefore — Put to death, slay with a continued stroke. Your members - Which together make up the body of sin. Which are upon the earth - Where they find their nourishment. Uncleanness - In act, word, or thought. Inordinate affection - Every passion which does not flow from and lead to the love of God. Evil desire - The desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life. Covetousness - According to the derivation of the word, means the desire of having more, or of any thing independent on God. Which is idolatry - Properly and directly; for it is giving the heart to a creature.
For which — Though the heathens lightly regarded them.
Living denotes the inward principle; walking, the outward acts.

Wrath — Is lasting anger. Filthy discourse - And was there need to warn even these saints of God against so gross and palpable a sin as this? O what is man, till perfect love casts out both fear and sin.
In knowledge — The knowledge of God, his will, his word.

Where — In which case, it matters not what a man is externally, whether Jew or gentile, circumcised, or uncircumcised, barbarian, void of all the advantages of education, yea, Scythian, of all barbarians most barbarous. But Christ is in all that are thus renewed, and is all things in them and to them.

glossa.text: *The things that are above.* Not by place, but by merit of excellence.
*The things above.* Spiritual things, which were signified through the carnal observances, these are eternal glory and the things which lead to it.

*Your life hidden.* That is, your time has not yet come, because the summer has not yet come, that is, the coming of Christ, where the fruitful trees shall be discerned from the barren; but the time of those who love earthly things is always ready. But when Christ shall have appeared, this is our time.

*Mortify,* etc. After the reasonings concerning the fulness of Christ, a general exhortation to all concerning morals is subjoined, lest they return to their former habit. *Your members.* That is, the parts of the old man, or the concupiscences of the members. *Fornication,* etc. He describes the offences which he calls members, that after receiving the reason of truth they might give their labour to a good life. It much harms to know the reason of the true, and not to carry it out in deeds. *For he who knows the will of the Lord, and does not do it, shall be beaten with many stripes ((Luc. XII))*. *And covetousness.* Under one name he forbids two most evil things, idolatry and covetousness, which is not a dissimilar wickedness, because it is the root of all evils, and they are fulfilled in almost one work: because, as idolatry strives to take glory away from the one God, lest he alone should have the name of deity, so the covetous man extends himself into the things of God, that he alone may usurp what God made for all: both are hostile to God, because they deny to God the things which are his.
*In which you also walked.* He mentions this, that they may rejoice that they have escaped, and may beware for the rest.

*But now.* Above he forbade the graver things, now the lesser, lest these be thought not dangerous. There are those who have not the habit of drunkenness, who sometimes get drunk: as also there are those who have not the habit of lying, and yet sometimes lie, so it happens in other matters also. He forbids therefore to lie sometimes, and especially to lie continually.

*Who is renewed.* The renewal of the mind is said to be according to God, as is read in the epistle to the Ephesians, or *according to the image of God,* as is read here. But it is said according to God for this reason, lest it be thought to come about according to some other creature.

notes.text: Who made me a judge? — In worldly things. His kingdom is not of this world.
He said to them — Perhaps to the two brothers, and through them to the people. A man's life - That is, the comfort or happiness of it.
What shall I do? — The very language of want! Do? Why, lay up treasure in heaven.
Thou fool — To think of satisfying thy soul with earthly goods! To depend on living many years! Yea, one day! They - The messengers of death, commissioned by God, require thy soul of thee!
Rich toward God — Namely, in faith, and love, and good works.

glossa.text: *Master.* Upon one who was commending the grace of the peace and unity above, this man wishes to thrust the trouble of an earthly division; whence also he is called a man, that is, earthly. For those among whom there is a zeal and contention of this kind are men, and walk according to man. Among brethren it is not a judge in the midst but family affection as arbitress that ought to divide a patrimony, although the patrimony of immortality is not money to be sought by men.

*Who hath appointed me.* I am not the God of dissension but of peace and unity, who came to make men at peace with the angels, that many may have one heart and one soul. Not that they may be divided, but that they may have all things in common, and that there be not anyone in need among them. He who does not gather with me is a divider of brotherhood and an author of dissension.

*Of all covetousness.* No one would think it a crime to divide an inheritance, to gather fruits into barns; but the judge above declares that this too is covetousness, whence also he adds: *of a certain rich man.* As above against the Pharisees and hypocrites, so here, on the occasion of a foolish petition, he disputes against covetousness. *Not in abundance. Man liveth not by bread alone, but in the word of God ((Deut. VIII))* , nor is temporal life prolonged by a multitude of riches.

*And he spoke,* etc. After the precept he subjoins an example for the avoiding of covetousness for temporal things. *The plentiful fruits of a certain rich man.* The rich man is not blamed because he tilled the ground, or laid up his fruits in barns, but because he placed the confidence of his life in them, and did not lay them out upon the poor, that he might be received by them into everlasting dwellings.

*What shall I do,* etc. Reckoning the fruits to be his own and the goods his own, he does not lay out upon the poor what is over and above, but is eager to keep it for his own luxury against the time to come, and knows not who will make use of what he has gathered.

*My goods, and I will say. ((AMBR.))* Those are not a man's goods which he cannot carry away with him. For mercy alone is the companion of the dead.

*Take thy rest.* Behold, to the plague of covetousness is joined the plague of sloth, so that he did not even call upon God for temporal things.

*But he said.* For God to speak is to check a man's depraved contrivances by a sudden chastisement. *Thou fool.* Because thou wast promising thyself long seasons of riches, this night, snatched away, thou shalt leave to others what thou hast gathered. *They require,* etc. In the night the soul is taken away, which in the darkness of the heart would not foresee what it could suffer.

*And is not rich toward God.* He is rich toward God who, despising things transitory, distributes to the poor; whose expectation is the Lord; whose substance, that is, the possession of a conscience by which he is sustained and fed, is with God, not in the purses of earth.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: "Where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God" verbally echoes the LXX of Ps 110:1 ("Sit at my right hand"), the most-cited OT verse in the NT. High volume of distinctive language (right hand, seated, exaltation) and strong recurrence make the session at God's right hand the dominant figure for the exalted Christ. Coherence with Colossians' cosmic Christology is exact.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The exalted Christ glorified and revealed in heavenly session may faintly invoke Daniel's Son of Man given dominion and glory before the Ancient of Days. Low volume since no distinctive vocabulary is reproduced; the echo rests on the shared schema of heavenly enthronement and future revelation "in glory" (v.4).

echoes.text: You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory. Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
echoes.note: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God" coheres with the psalmist's hope that God is his portion and will receive him to glory, the hidden security of life bound to God. Faint and contested; rests on thematic coherence (hiddenness, glory, God as the believer's life) rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: "Covetousness, which is idolatry" presupposes the Decalogue's prohibition of coveting, the climactic command that exposes disordered desire. The identification of greed with idolatry draws on Israel's covenant logic where craving what is not one's own is functionally false worship; coherent with Second-Temple Jewish moralizing of pleonexia.

echoes.text: “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
echoes.note: Naming covetousness "idolatry" invokes the first commandment's exclusive worship and the prohibition of other gods. The equation of greed with idol-service is a recurring Second-Temple move (cf. Testament traditions) grounded in the Decalogue's opening; coheres with the wrath-of-God indictment that follows.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: "Evil desire" and the inventory of corrupt members recall the prophetic-Pentateuchal diagnosis that the inclination of the human heart is only evil continually. Faint; the vice list is a Hellenistic-Jewish form and contact is conceptual (the earthly members, depraved passion) rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Remember, and don’t forget, how you provoked Yahweh your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day that you left the land of Egypt, until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against Yahweh.
echoes.note: "The wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience" coheres with Deuteronomy's recurring theme of divine wrath provoked by Israel's rebellion and idolatry. Faint and generic; the wrath-against-disobedience schema is pervasive across the prophets, so no single passage controls.

echoes.text: Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab; for they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods. The people ate and bowed down to their gods. Israel joined himself to Baal Peor. Yahweh’s anger was kindled against Israel. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take all the chiefs of the people, and hang them up to Yahweh before the sun, that the fierce anger of Yahweh may turn away from Israel.” Moses said to […]
echoes.note: Linking sexual immorality and idolatry, followed by divine wrath, echoes the Baal-Peor episode where harlotry with Moab and idol-worship together kindle God's anger. Faint; contact is the recurrent OT pairing of porneia with idolatry under wrath rather than verbal citation.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: "The new man, being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator" directly reworks the creation of humanity in God's image. High volume (image, Creator, the making of man) and exact coherence: the new self is re-creation according to the imago Dei, recapitulating Gen 1. Availability and recurrence in Pauline new-creation theology are strong.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not steal. “‘You shall not lie. “‘You shall not deceive one another.
echoes.note: "Don't lie to one another" closely tracks the Holiness Code's "you shall not lie one to another" (LXX), addressed to the covenant community. Strong verbal and situational coherence (reciprocal prohibition among the people of God); the holiness framing fits Colossians' renewed humanity.

echoes.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness.
echoes.note: "After the image of his Creator" also resonates with the toledot statement that God made man in his likeness, the verse that reasserts the image after the fall. Supports the renewal-of-the-image reading; medium because Gen 1:26-27 is the primary lexical source and 5:1 is the secondary, reinforcing one.

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: "There can't be Greek and Jew... but Christ is all and in all" figurally reconstitutes the single humanity created in God's image, undoing the divisions of the nations. The renewed image (vv.10) grounds a restored one-humanity; coheres with Gen 1's making of mankind as a unity before the scattering of Babel.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard the voice of Yahweh God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden. Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I […]
echoes.note: "Put off the old man... put on the new" with its clothing imagery may figurally invoke Adam: the garments and the postlapsarian self stripped off. Faint and contested; the old-man/new-man Adam typology is conceptual, and the clothing metaphor is widely diffused in Jewish moral discourse.

echoes.text: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said one to another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole […]
echoes.note: The catalog of peoples (Greek, Jew, barbarian, Scythian) reconciled in Christ faintly reverses Babel's scattering and confusion of tongues into many nations. Low volume; the reversal-of-Babel reading is thematic and contested, resting on the restoration of one humanity rather than any cited wording.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?'—the Hebrew's rebuke of Moses—is verbally echoed in Jesus' 'Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?' The near-quotation of the question gives notable Volume, though the speaker roles are inverted, marking it a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
echoes.note: 'Whoever loves money will not be satisfied with money'—Qoheleth's verdict on the futility of abundance—coheres directly with 'a man's life doesn't consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.' The wisdom critique of accumulation supports the warning against covetousness.

echoes.text: If a man has two wives, the one beloved, and the other hated, and they have borne him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son is hers who was hated; then it shall be, in the day that he causes his sons to inherit that which he has, that he may not give the son of the beloved the rights of the firstborn before the son of the hated, who is the firstborn; but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated, by giving him a […]
echoes.note: The Torah law of inheritance division among heirs supplies the legal backdrop for the brother's request to divide the inheritance. It is the unstated Availability rather than an allusion Luke develops, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: There is that waxes rich by his wariness and pinching, And this is the portion of his reward: When he says, I have found rest, And now will I eat of my goods; Yet he knows not what time will pass, And he will leave them to others, and die.
echoes.note: Ben Sira describes one who grows rich, says 'I have found rest, now I will enjoy my goods,' yet does not know his death is near and must leave them to others. This is the closest Second-Temple template for the rich fool: the inner monologue of ease, the unexpected death, and the unanswered 'whose will they be,' giving very high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's refrain that there is nothing better than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment underlies the rich fool's 'take your ease, eat, drink, be merry.' Luke ironizes the wisdom counsel by exposing its folly when death intervenes, giving strong thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
echoes.note: 'I commend enjoyment, for man has nothing better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry' is virtually quoted in the fool's resolve. The verbal triad eat/drink/be merry makes this a direct verbal source, though Luke subverts it.

echoes.text: “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.
echoes.note: 'He heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather it' is closely echoed by God's 'the things you have prepared—whose will they be?' The psalm's lament over the futility of hoarding against death gives strong Coherence and good Volume.

echoes.text: As the partridge that sits on eggs which she has not laid, so is he who gets riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days they shall leave him, and at his end he shall be a fool.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's proverb that one who gets riches unjustly will leave them in the midst of his days and prove a fool at his end supplies both the 'fool' verdict and the premature loss of wealth. The shared fool-and-forfeited-riches motif gives notable Coherence.

echoes.text: For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
echoes.note: 'What is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?' parallels the question posed to the rich man whose soul is required. The taking of the life of the prosperous-but-godless undergirds the parable's verdict.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him. Though while he lived he blessed his soul— and men praise you when you do well for yourself— he shall go to the generation of his fathers. They shall never see the light. A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.
echoes.note: The psalm warns not to fear the rich who lay up wealth, for they carry nothing away at death and perish like the beasts. The 'man in his pomp who does not understand' is a near-portrait of the rich fool, giving good Coherence to 'not rich toward God.'

echoes.text: “If I have made gold my hope, and have said to the fine gold, ‘You are my confidence;’ If I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because my hand had gotten much; if I have seen the sun when it shined, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for I should have denied the God who is above.
echoes.note: Job's disavowal of making gold his hope reflects the parable's contrast between trusting accumulated wealth and being 'rich toward God.' The trust-in-riches-as-folly theme is a coherent but lighter echo.

echoes.text: Wakefulness that comes of riches consumes the flesh, And the anxiety thereof puts away sleep. Wakeful anxiety will crave slumber; And in a sore disease sleep will be broken. A rich man toileth in gathering money together; And when he rests, he is filled with his good things. A poor man toileth in lack of substance; And when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's reflections on wealth, sleepless anxiety over riches, and the rare rich man who is blameless complement the parable's critique of storing goods. A faint Second-Temple coherence echo behind the barn-building scheme.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Give thanks to the Lord, who is good.
God's steadfast love endures forever.
You taught us to walk, and lifted us like a child to your cheek.
We were held, and we did not know it.
A man filled his barns and called his soul safe — but the barns could not keep him.
Make us rich toward God, not toward ourselves.
Come, you whom the Lord has gathered, and worship.
We give thanks, for God is good. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Remember a parent crouched a few steps away, arms open, coaxing a wobbling toddler forward — that is how God taught Israel to walk.
God's steadfast love endures forever.
Bent down to feed them, lifted them to the cheek, led them with cords of kindness — and they did not know who was holding them.
God's steadfast love endures forever.
Meanwhile a rich man tore down his barns to build bigger ones, sure he had years of ease stored up — and that very night his life was asked of him.
God's steadfast love endures forever.
So set down the hoarding and the worry, and let yourself be gathered and fed by the One whose arms have held you all along.
God's steadfast love endures forever. Thanks be to God!
